1:
Keil and Delitzsch explain why the verse is built as it is: the elaborate genealogy of Kish and the minute description of his son's figure are meant to indicate at the very outset the importance to which Saul attained in relation to the people of Israel. Ellicott sets the chapter against what precedes it — the compiler, having told how the elders asked the last of the judges for a king and were sent home to await the result of his communing with the Eternal, now opens the account of the man to be anointed with a short notice of his family and a word of personal description. Gill notes only that the tribe took its name from the youngest son of Jacob, and that one of it was the first king of Israel.

The lineage itself is tangled, and the two who work at it do not agree. Keil and Delitzsch make Kish the son of Abiel, which agrees with the later notice of Saul's house (1 Samuel 14:51); where the Chronicles say instead that Ner begat Kish, they reconcile the difference by supposing that Ner is there not the father but the grandfather, or a more remote ancestor still, intervening members being frequently passed over in genealogies (1 Chronicles 8:33). The rest of Kish's ancestors, they add, are never mentioned again. Ellicott instead sets out a line that keeps Ner between Abiel and Kish, reading the summaries together (Genesis 46:21; 1 Chronicles 7:6), and allows that even so certain links are missing, since a Matri and a Jehiel appear elsewhere (1 Samuel 10:21; 1 Chronicles 9:35). His explanation is editorial rather than textual: in each summary the transcriber left out names not needed for his particular purpose, and the names omitted are not always the same, which is where the apparent discrepancies come from. Dean Payne Smith, whom he quotes, lays the entanglement of the Benjamite genealogies partly at the door of the terrible civil war that followed the crime recorded in Judges, in whose massacres many of the older tribal records must have perished (Judges 20:1).

What kind of power Kish had is read three ways. Keil and Delitzsch deny it means a brave man and take it for a man of property, the phrase bearing that sense elsewhere (Ruth 2:1). Clarke renders it literally a strong man and adds, drily, that this appears to be the only power he possessed — while suggesting that the physical strength of the father may account for the extraordinary size of the son. Henry takes all three senses at once, following the margin's "in substance": bold in spirit, strong in body, wealthy in estate. Ellicott simply calls him a noble and opulent Benjamite of Gibeah.

The tribe matters as much as the family. Henry recalls that Benjamin had been reduced to a very small number by the fatal war with Gibeah, so that there was much ado to provide wives for the six hundred men who were its poor remains — the tribe is called, with good reason, the smallest of the tribes of Israel, and Saul sprang as a root out of a dry ground. Yet though fewest in number it was first in dignity, God giving more abundant honour to the part that lacked (1 Corinthians 12:24); and since the whole lot of Benjamin came to be divided among six hundred men, Henry supposes their inheritances were much larger than other men's, an advantage that somewhat balanced the smallness of their number. He notices too that the New Testament Saul was of the same tribe and counted it his honour (Romans 11:1; Philippians 3:5), a comparison Gill makes as well, though to mark the difference — that Saul was a little man, this one large and tall.
2:
The first of the two epithets will not carry the weight the English gives it. Ellicott points out that one Hebrew word cannot signify both "choice" and "young," and supposes the translators were influenced by the Latin, which renders it electus — the commoner sense of the word being avoided because Saul appears by this time to have had a son, Jonathan, who must have been near maturity. Yet "young" is not inappropriate, he argues, since Saul was still in the full vigour of manhood, about forty to forty-five years old, as against the old age of Samuel; so he would translate simply "a young man."

On the stature all of them agree, and all explain it the same way. Clarke thinks it was probably from this very circumstance that Saul was chosen, since where kings were elective great respect was paid in all ancient times to personal appearance. Wesley says much the same of a tall stature, that it was greatly valued in a king in ancient times and in the eastern countries. Ellicott observes that in the childhood of nations heroic proportions were highly valued, and that the gigantic stature and remarkable beauty of the king no doubt helped the ready acceptance of the young Benjamite by a still semi-barbarous Israel — a point he supports from Herodotus and Aristotle and from the descriptions of Turnus in Virgil and of Ajax in Homer. Gill notes the contrast with the later Saul of the same tribe, a little man where this one was large and tall, perhaps like his father.

Henry reads the description for what it leaves out. No mention is made of Saul's wisdom or virtue, his learning or piety, or any accomplishment of mind — only that he was a tall, proper, handsome man with a good face, a good shape and a good presence, graceful and well proportioned, taller by head and shoulders than any of the people, as if nature had marked him for pre-eminence, and the fitter to be a match for the giants of Gath. When God chose a king after his own heart he pitched on one not at all remarkable for height, with nothing in his countenance but the innocence and sweetness that appeared there; but when he chose a king after the people's heart, who aimed at nothing so much as stateliness and grandeur, he pitched on this huge tall man, who if he had no other good qualities would at least look great. Nor does Saul appear to have excelled in strength as he did in stature, Henry adds: Samson did, and him they slighted and bound and betrayed into Philistine hands, so they are justly now put off with one who, though of uncommon height, is weak as other men. They would have a king like the nations, and the nations commonly chose portly men for their kings.

Keil and Delitzsch pass straight from the description to the errand, reading the two verses as one introduction: having been sent out by his father to search for the she-asses that had strayed, Saul went with his servant through the mountains of Ephraim, which run southwards into the territory of Benjamin, and so into the search that occupies the rest of the chapter.
3:
Gill states the loss plainly — the animals had got out of the stables or fields where they were kept and strayed. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew has the she-asses, and that these, belonging to the farm of Kish and probably kept for breeding, were untethered and so wandered from the neighbourhood and were lost.

Why asses were worth a search at all is explained from the economy. Clarke observes that asses grow to great perfection in the East, and that at this time, there being no horses in Judea, they were very useful, and kings and princes rode on them. Wesley says the same of their price — great, because of the scarcity of horses — and concludes that they were therefore not held unworthy of Saul's seeking, at least in those ancient times when simplicity, humility and industry were in fashion among persons of quality. Ellicott adds the legal ground of that scarcity, the horse being forbidden by the Law, and points out how widely asses served: not only for agriculture but for riding, as in the song about those who ride on white asses, and as the thirty sons of the Gileadite judge each rode an ass colt (Judges 5:10; Judges 10:4).

Whether the chain of events was providence or coincidence is where Clarke and Henry pull apart. Clarke marvels at the train of occurrences connected to bring Saul to the throne: everything seems to go on according to the common course of events, and yet all conspired to favour the election of a man to the kingdom who certainly did not come there by the approbation of God. Henry reads the same smallness as design. Saul had no preferment at all, nor any post of honour or trust, until he was chosen king; most who are advanced rise gradually, but Saul stepped at once from the level of his neighbours into the throne, according to Hannah's word that God raiseth up the poor out of the dust to set them among princes (1 Samuel 2:8). Promotion comes not by chance nor by human probabilities, Henry concludes, but God is the Judge — and a great event here arises from very small occurrences.

The errand itself Henry turns into a series of homely lessons. Perhaps there was no way to give public notice that a number of asses had strayed; there was a good law obliging a man to bring back a neighbour's straying ox or ass, but it is to be feared that law was neglected like other good ones. Those who have must expect to lose, it is wisdom to look after what is lost, no man should think it below him to know the state of his flocks, and children should be forward to serve their parents' interests. Saul's taking care of the asses, however, Henry ascribes not so much to humility of spirit as to the plainness and simplicity of those times — his obedience to his father is the commendable part. Seest thou a man diligent in his business and dutiful to his superiors, willing to stoop and to take pains? He stands fair for preferment, as Saul did. And the choice of companion was deliberate: the servant of Kish would be faithful only as a servant, where Saul would be faithful as a son, in his own family's business, and therefore the servant was sent with him. Ellicott says a good deal for that servant too — the word is servant and not slave, and he was evidently a trusty dependant of the house, on familiar terms with his young master, who gives wise advice in the course of the search, carries the money, and is afterwards treated by Samuel as an honoured guest at the sacrificial feast.
4:
The circuit of the search is traced as far as the names allow. Gill takes Mount Ephraim for the mountainous part of that tribe, lying next to Benjamin, where the asses might be supposed to have strayed; Ellicott notes that the chain ran southward into the territory of Benjamin, where the patrimonial possessions of Saul's house lay. Shalisha he explains as the land "of the Three," so called because three valleys there united in one, or one divided into three, and identifies it with the region in which Baal-shalisha lay, fifteen miles north of Lydda (2 Kings 4:42); Shalim he takes for a very deep valley, from a Hebrew word signifying the hollow of the hand; and Zuph he believes to have been in the south-west of Benjamin. Gill identifies Zuph by its chief town, the Ramathaim-zophim that was Samuel's birthplace, and cites the Targum's rendering — the land in which was the prophet.

Clarke sets out a route and then withdraws his confidence in it. Calmet, he reports, supposes they went from Gibeah to Shalisha in the tribe of Dan, thence to Shalim near Jerusalem, and thence through Benjamin, meaning to return to Gibeah, but passing through the land of Zuph where Ramatha lay they determined to call on the prophet — the whole circuit amounting, on that reckoning, to no more than about twenty-five leagues, or three days' journey. Yet we do not know where the places were situated, Clarke says flatly, and the Targum he quotes gives quite different names, carrying Saul through the mount of the house of Ephraim into the southern land and then through the land of Mathbera before he reaches the country where the prophet of the LORD dwelt.

Henry marks the failure of the errand and its outcome together: Saul and his servant travelled far, probably on foot, in quest of the asses and found them not, so he missed what he sought — and yet had no reason to complain of the disappointment, for he met with the kingdom, which he never dreamed of.

Why Saul turned back when he did is read as a point of character. Keil and Delitzsch give the reason from the text, that he feared his father would leave off caring for the asses and begin to be troubled about the searchers themselves. Ellicott quotes Dr Kitto's verdict on it — Saul's tender regard for his father's feelings here is a favourable indication of character. Henry fills in what the old man would have feared, as Jacob feared concerning Joseph, that an evil beast had devoured them or some mischief befallen them, and turns it into a charge: children should take care to do nothing that would grieve or frighten their parents, but be tender of their tenderness.
6:
The proposal comes from the servant, as Gill is careful to note, and Keil and Delitzsch catch the gesture in the Hebrew: "in this city" points at the town standing in front of them upon a hill. Ellicott fills out the scene — the servant pointing to the tower of the then famous residence of the seer and judge, and asking whether his master will not enquire of him about the missing beasts.

Whether such a question was fit to put to such a man is the real matter here, and the three answers run from approval to rebuke. Ellicott takes the servant's simplicity as evidence of something admirable: the young countryman thought the loss of his master's asses occasion enough to warrant intruding on the prophet-judge of Israel, and the relation between Samuel and the people must have been very close and friendly for that to occur to him at all — it says much for the old prophet's kindly, unselfish disposition that his name was so loved and honoured even in the secluded farms of the Land of Promise. Wesley hears hesitation rather than confidence in the servant's "peradventure": he doubted whether so great a prophet would seek, or God would grant him, a revelation about such mean matters, though God was sometimes pleased to condescend so far, to cut off all occasion of resorting to heathenish divination. Henry is blunt. All the use they proposed to make of the man of God was to learn whether to go home or which way to turn next — a poor business to employ a prophet about. Had they said, let us give the asses up for lost and, being near the man of God, go and learn from him the good knowledge of God, the proposal would have become Israelites; but to make prophecy serve so mean a turn discovered too much what manner of spirit they were of. Most people, he adds, would rather be told their fortune than their duty, how to be rich than how to be saved.

On the title the servant gives Samuel all three agree. Ellicott would render it "one held in honour" rather than "an honourable man"; Wesley takes it of great reputation for skill and faithfulness, and draws the general rule that acquaintance with God and serviceableness to the kingdom of God make men truly honourable. Henry says the same and adds what is remarkable in the speaker: the servant spoke very respectfully of Samuel though he knew him only by common fame. Men of God are honourable men and should be so in our eyes, since acquaintance with the things of God and usefulness to his kingdom put true honour upon men and make them great. And the particular honour claimed here — that all he says comes surely to pass — was observed of Samuel when he was still a young prophet, God letting none of his words fall to the ground (1 Samuel 3:19).

Henry draws one more thing from the mere accident of their position. They were close by the city where Samuel lived, and that put it into their heads to consult him; so wherever we are we should improve our opportunities of acquainting ourselves with those who are wise and good — though many will consult a man of God if he comes in their way who would not go a step out of their way to get wisdom.
7:
Saul's objection is practical: the bread in their vessels is spent, so they have nothing to bring. Keil and Delitzsch state it so and let the servant answer it out of his own pocket, with the quarter shekel he happens to be carrying, so that the obstacle Saul raised is removed by the servant and not by him. Gill finds a further hesitation under it, following the Targum's rendering — "if he receives money" — which he takes to mean that Saul was not clear whether Samuel accepted such things at all: certain persons who set up for prophets did, and a sort of diviners and fortune-tellers, but whether so eminent and honourable a man did, Saul could not tell, having no such knowledge of Samuel, who had judged Israel so many years, as would settle the question either way.

What a present to such a man signified is where most of the comment lies. Clarke denies flatly that the prophets took money to predict future events: Saul refers only to the invariable custom that no man approached a superior without a present of some kind — even God, who needs nothing, would not have his people approach him with empty hands — and he supports it from Ward's account of Bengal, where one who wishes to ask a favour of a superior takes fruits or sweetmeats in his hand, and the offerer's feelings are greatly wounded if the gift is not accepted. Ellicott agrees that it would seem strange at first for one like Samuel to be approached with gifts, but says the custom was in many cases an act of respectful homage rather than a fee, and sets beside it the spicery Jacob sent to Pharaoh's great minister (Genesis 43:11), the ten cheeses Jesse sent to the captain of the thousand in which his sons served, and the gifts the Queen of Sheba brought Solomon (1 Kings 10:10). Wesley multiplies the possible purposes: a testimony of respect, a grateful acknowledgement, the support of the prophets themselves or of the sons of the prophets, or relief of others in want known to them.
8:
Henry weighs a harsher reading before rejecting it. Some think that when Saul talked of a fee he measured Samuel by himself, or by Samuel's sons, as though the man must be hired to do an honest Israelite a kindness, and was like the false prophets who divined for money (Micah 3:11) — coming to him as to a fortune-teller rather than a prophet, and therefore reckoning a quarter of a shekel enough. But Henry judges it rather agreeable to the general usage of those times, and to natural equity, that those who sow spiritual things should reap temporal things from those for whom they labour. Samuel needed not their money and would not have withheld his advice had they brought none; it is probable he gave it to the poor; they brought it as a token of respect and of the value they set on his office, and he did not refuse it, for they could afford it, and little as it was, it was the widow's mite. They could not bring loaves and cakes as Jeroboam's wife brought Ahijah (1 Kings 14:3), their own provision being gone.

What the coin was worth nobody quite agrees. Clarke reckons the fourth part of a shekel at about ninepence of our money and concludes that the present was meant more as a token of respect than as an emolument, noting that had their bread not been spent a part of that would have been thought suitable. Henry puts it at about sevenpence halfpenny. Ellicott declines the calculation altogether, quoting Dean Payne Smith: the shekel was probably roughly stamped and divided into four quarters by a cross, to be broken when needed, and what its proportionate value was in Samuel's days we cannot tell, for silver then was rare.

Henry keeps one sting for Saul. As he never thought of going to the man of God till the servant proposed it, so he seems to have mentioned the want of a present as an objection against going at all, not owning that he had money of his own; and only when the servant generously offered to bear the charge did he say, well said, come, let us go. Most people love a cheap religion, Henry remarks, and like it best when they can devolve the expense of it on others.
9:
Everyone treats this verse as an interruption, and nearly all as a later hand. Keil and Delitzsch describe it as a notice the historian introduces before carrying the affair further, to throw light on what follows. Clarke goes further: the passage could not have been part of the book originally, which fits his conjecture that Samuel or a contemporary wrote the memoranda out of which a later author compiled it — a hypothesis he thinks reasonable in itself and solving all difficulties of the kind. Ellicott agrees it was evidently inserted into the original book of memoirs by a later hand, perhaps in the time of Ezra, but insists the inserter must have been a reviser of very high authority, since the note has come down to us as an integral part of the received Hebrew text. Wesley alone leaves the alternative open: either the words of some later sacred writer who inserted the verse after Samuel's death, or of Samuel himself, who, being perhaps fifty or sixty when the book was written and speaking of the state of things in his first days, might well call it beforetime.

Clarke adds a question of placing rather than authorship: he thinks the verse comes in more naturally after the eleventh.

Why the note was needed at all Ellicott explains from the history of the words. Three terms serve in these writings for the inspired interpreters of the Eternal will, and seer was the most ancient of them — evidently the title by which Samuel was generally known in his lifetime, as the questions and answers of this very chapter show. As time passed the word lost that sense and another, meaning a gazer on strange visions, came into use for an inspired man; while the term prophet, found in nearly all the books from Genesis to Malachi though rarely in the earlier ones, began to come into common use in Samuel's own day. The scribe's purpose, Ellicott concludes, was to point out that when Samuel lived "seer" was the word always used for a prophet of the LORD, before it had deteriorated in meaning.

Clarke works the same ground differently. The word occurs here for the first time, and literally signifies a person who sees, particularly preternatural sights; a seer and a prophet were the same in most cases, with this difference, that the seer was always a prophet but the prophet not always a seer, a seer seeming to imply one who frequently met with and saw some symbolical representation of God. The term prophet was in use long before — Abraham is so called (Genesis 20:7) — and occurs often in the law, whereas seer does not appear before this place and then recurs through the prophets for more than three hundred years (Amos 7:12; Micah 3:7). All prophets, false and true, profess to see God, as Balaam did (Numbers 24:4; Jeremiah 14:14), and all diviners in their enthusiastic flights boasted that things to come were exhibited to their sight — for which Clarke offers Virgil's Sibyl as a specimen, professing herself a seer of wars and of a river foaming with blood.

The simplest readings come from Gill and Wesley. Gill takes inquiring of God to be asking doctrine of him, as the Targum has it — to be taught by him and learn his mind in any affair of moment — usually done by applying to some man of God eminent for grace and piety and a spirit of prophecy. Wesley derives the title from the function: seer, because he discerned and could discover things secret and unknown to others. Henry turns it on those who would hold the office: those that are prophets must first be seers, for whoever undertakes to speak to others of the things of God must have an insight into those things himself.
10:
Saul's assent is warmer in the Hebrew than the English lets on. Gill renders it "good is thy word" — thou hast well spoken, it is a good proposal, and thou art very generous to give all thou hast to the man — and adds the hope that moved him: since he is a seer, he may tell them where the asses are, or which way to take to find them, so that things look feasible enough. Keil and Delitzsch report the assent flatly: Saul declared himself satisfied with the servant's answer, and the two went into the town to ask the man of God about the lost asses.

Which town it was the narrative never says, and Ellicott builds a case for the obvious answer. The impression the story leaves is that it was Samuel's usual residence, Ramah, and four things point that way: Samuel had built an altar to the LORD at Ramah (1 Samuel 7:17); on the day of Saul's arrival a great sacrifice was taking place on the altar of the high place of the city; in this nameless city the seer had a house of his own, as the later verses show; and Samuel was known to Saul's servant as dwelling in this place.

What they went up to is a detail Keil and Delitzsch will not let pass. The word rendered "the hill" is not the height or hill generally but, throughout, the high place as a place of sacrifice or prayer — so that the two men climbing towards the town were climbing towards its sanctuary, which is where the maidens' answer will send them.

Gill derives the city’s name from the climb itself: it was built upon a hill, whence it was called Ramah, a word signifying high and lifted up. Keil and Delitzsch set the meeting at that point — as the two were going up to the high place of the town they met maidens coming out of it to draw water, and asked them whether the seer was there.

Clarke takes the encounter as evidence about ordinary life. So far is it from being true that young women were always kept closely shut up at home, that we find them often in the field, drawing and carrying water, as here. Henry values the maidens for their usefulness: the maidservants of Ramah could give Saul and his servant intelligence about Samuel, and were very particular in their directions — from which he draws the rule that we should always be ready to give what help we can to those enquiring after God’s prophets, and to further them in their enquiries.

That Saul had to ask at all strikes Henry as remarkable. Gibeah of Saul was not twenty miles from Ramah where Samuel dwelt, and lay near Mizpeh where he often judged Israel, and yet Saul had lived so privately and taken so little notice of public affairs that he had never seen the man: when they met he did not know him. One advantage follows from that ignorance, Henry allows — there was no cause to suspect any secret compact or collusion between them in the matter of the kingdom, and he sets beside it the Baptist’s word about Christ, I knew him not (John 1:31). But he will not turn it into praise: he does not think it any commendation to Saul that he was a stranger to Samuel.
12:
Ellicott hears an eye-witness in the exchange. The little scene, in itself in no way remarkable, is recounted as introducing momentous consequences, every detail of that day's proceedings being of deep interest to Israel: some of the maidens of Ramah are at the well side drawing water for their homes, the two strangers accost them to ask whether the seer who dwells among them is there just now, and they reply eagerly that this very day he came from his house into the town, that it is a festival day, and that he will be found presiding up there — pointing to the high place where the sacrifices were being offered. Every word spoken by those girls, who loved to display their local knowledge and their interest in their great fellow-citizen, was remembered afterwards by Saul and his companion. Gill keeps to the plain sense: he is in the city, at home, and to be spoken with.

Where Samuel had come from that day is answered three ways. Clarke notes that though he lived chiefly in Ramah he had a dwelling in the country at a place called Naioth, where it is probable there was a school of the prophets (1 Samuel 19:18). Wesley has him returning from travels abroad to his own house in Ramah. Henry allows either, from his circuit or from his country seat, and adds the reason the maidens knew at all: he was such a public person that his movements were generally known.

The high place and its sacrifice are explained as an irregularity licensed by the times. Henry points out that the tabernacle, being deprived of the ark, no longer had the reputation it once held, nor were the people confined to it as they would be when God again chose a place to put his name in, so that other places were allowed — and Samuel had built an altar at Ramah which is here in use (1 Samuel 7:17). Clarke thinks the high place means probably Samuel's altar alone, no doubt raised on an eminence, and describes the occasion as a great feast in which the animals were first sacrificed to the LORD, their blood poured out before him, and then the people fed on the flesh. Wesley places it on the hill just mentioned, near that same altar. Clarke adds a living parallel: among the Arabs a large feast is often made of sacrificed camels and the neighbourhood invited to partake, which is the custom alluded to in the bidding of guests.

Why nobody would eat before Samuel arrived turns on what his blessing was. Keil and Delitzsch take the Hebrew verb of the thanksgiving prayer offered before the sacrificial meal, and render the clause as a statement of custom — the people are not accustomed to eat till he comes, for he blesses the sacrifice. Wesley divides that blessing in two, thanksgiving, this being a thank-offering, and prayer to God for its acceptance. Clarke makes it a matter of office rather than of grace before meat: he alone can perform the religious rites used on this occasion. Ellicott takes the opposite view of its significance, finding here a very early instance of the devout Hebrew practice of asking a blessing on meals.

Two small observations close the maidens' directions. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word opening the promise is used of time, in the sense of our "immediately" — the seekers will find him directly, before he goes up to eat. Gill infers from the same promptness that Samuel's house stood at the end of the city by which they entered, which agrees with the maidens' saying that he was before them, his house being in sight. Wesley reads the timing as hospitality: they would find him at home and at leisure.
14:
The meeting happens at the gate, as it were by accident. Gill has Saul and his servant go up the hill to the city of Ramah; Keil and Delitzsch note that as they went in, Samuel met them on his own way out to the high place of sacrifice. Before describing the encounter itself, they observe, the historian breaks off to tell us what had passed the day before — that the LORD had foretold to Samuel the coming of the man he was to anoint as captain over his people.

Two phrases in that foretelling Keil and Delitzsch gloss. To open a man's ear is the Hebrew way of saying that something was revealed to him, as elsewhere in the history of David (1 Samuel 20:12; 2 Samuel 7:27); and the promise "I will send thee" they gloss, on the authority they cite as J. H. Mich., to mean that God would so direct the man's way in his overruling providence that he should come to Samuel. They also answer an objection in advance: the words about saving the people out of the hand of the Philistines are not at variance with the earlier account of Philistine subjection, which asserts only that there was no longer any permanent oppression.

Ellicott frames the whole encounter with a long passage from Ewald, and it is worth following because it reads the scene as a study in two kinds of ignorance. Saul comes before Samuel bashfully pursuing his humble quest, in apparent unconsciousness of the power slumbering within him, of aspiring and attaining to the highest place; and the great seer receives him in a way quite different from anything he could have hoped or feared. At the moment of their meeting the seer has come out from his house towards the solitary sacred heights of the city where he lives, to sacrifice on the altar or to share a sacrificial repast with some of his closest friends. He at once desires to take Saul with him, telling him beforehand how unimportant the object of his enquiries was and that the matter was already settled, but that for him and his whole house a very different and far better destiny was reserved in Israel. And though Saul, in his unassuming simplicity, would gladly waive the honour so obscurely hinted — so little does he yet know his better self — the holy man, more discerning, takes him to the sacrificial meal already prepared, assigns him the place of honour among the thirty guests invited beforehand, and has him served with a portion of the sacrificial meat put by as if specially for him: for in like manner a portion other and higher than that of ordinary men had long been reserved for him by heaven.
15:
How the warning reached Samuel is where the voices differ most sharply, because the Hebrew idiom invites a picture and Clarke refuses to draw one. Ellicott translates literally — the LORD had uncovered the ear of Samuel — and explains the image from the action of pushing aside the head-dress the more conveniently to whisper into the ear; this, he says, is one of the few more direct intimations in the sacred records of a way in which the Spirit of God communicated divine thoughts to the human spirit, the Eternal Spirit being here represented as whispering in a man's ear. He quotes Ewald to the same effect, that the true Spirit of Jehovah, full of compassion, had already on the preceding day whispered to Samuel that a Benjamite must be anointed king for the deliverance of his people. Gill keeps the same picture without the archaeology: a private manner, a whispering in the ear, telling him in a free, familiar, friendly way, as a secret. Wesley hazards only that it was secret, perhaps by a still small voice. Clarke declines the question outright — how this communication was made, we cannot tell.

Gill reads the promise "I will send thee a man" as a study in unconscious providence. Saul would come without any thought or design of his own, merely directed by the providence of God, expecting no kingdom but at most news of his father's asses and the way to find them — and it was precisely his failure to find them that brought him there.

What Saul was to be anointed Clarke will not let the English flatten. The word is not king but captain, the leader of the LORD's host; and yet, he adds, in ancient times no king was esteemed who was not an able warrior, for which he produces Alexander's judgement that the truest line in the whole Iliad was the one calling Atrides great in the war and great in acts of sway.

Which enemy drove the demand for a king is a real disagreement. Ellicott makes it the Philistines: the statement here points to the fact, amply evidenced a little later, that at this juncture they were again harassing Israelite territory with destructive raids. Their power had been broken but by no means destroyed at Mizpeh, and through all Saul's reign and David's early days the invasions were repeated with varying success — so the earlier verse about their subjection must be read as saying that from that day their power began to decline, including the ultimate result of the victory rather than its immediate effect. The annoyance of those raids, he concludes, was the immediate cause of the prayer for a king: the desire for that form of government had existed a long while, but the pressing need of a younger and more warlike leader than their old prophet-judge prompted the request. Wesley puts the weight elsewhere. The people were at that moment most pressed by the Ammonites, but they looked on those as a land-flood, soon up and soon down again, whereas the Philistines were their constant and nearest enemies and the ones they most dreaded — and from these Saul did in some measure save them, and would have saved them much more had his sins and the people's not hindered. Keil and Delitzsch meet the same difficulty on textual ground, insisting the promise is not at variance with the earlier account, which asserts only that there was no longer any permanent oppression.
17:
Both Gill and Ellicott have Samuel put a silent question before he gets an answer. Gill supposes he could not but take notice of the stranger for his height, which might raise the suspicion that this was the man — the more so because it was the exact hour at which the man was to be sent — and so he fixed his eyes on him, wanting to be assured and left in no uncertainty. Ellicott makes the question explicit and reverent: the seer, at once impressed by the great stature and splendid beauty of the stranger coming towards him on his way to the sacred height, asks his Master silently whether this is he of whom the whisper came the day before, to whom the destinies of his people were to be confided; and the words "behold the man" were the silent answer of God to the silent prayer of his old servant. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same thing in one clause — the LORD answered him in reply to the tacit inquiry, Is this he?

Ellicott adds a reminder about the order of the narrative: this verse follows closely on the meeting at the gate, the two verses about the previous day's revelation being parenthetical.

Clarke draws from the exchange a conclusion about the man rather than the moment. What an intimate communion must Samuel have held with his God — a constant familiarity seems to have existed between them.

The last words of the verse are harsher in the Hebrew than in the English. The word, which Ellicott describes as whispered by the Spirit to the listening heart of the seer, he would not render "shall reign" at all but "shall control," or "shall restrain," and reads it as a word which, looking forward to what Saul's reign became, represented it as a stern, severe rule. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the same verb in Latin to the same effect, as the coercing of a people by authority — so that the sentence spoken over Saul at his first appearance already carries the character of the government he would exercise.
18:
Where exactly Saul came up with Samuel is a question of one Hebrew word, and three answers are on offer. Keil and Delitzsch defend the text as it stands: "in the gate" simply specifies more precisely the general statement that they came into the city, and there is no necessity to alter that earlier phrase to match, as Thenius proposes, since the words do not mean to be in the middle of the town, as he imagines, but to enter it — and the entrance to a town was through its gate. Ellicott leans the other way, noting that the Greek reads "in the midst of the city" and thinking it not improbable that this is the original, since a scribe might very easily write the Hebrew for gate in place of the Hebrew for city. Gill leaves the location open between two possibilities: either at the door of Samuel's own house, just as he was coming out of it, or within the city gate as Saul entered, Samuel coming to it on his way through to the high place, which was probably outside the town — which is why the narrative says he came out to meet them.

Keil and Delitzsch also note what the verse does to the narrative: the thread broken off before the account of the previous day's revelation is here picked up again.

The irony of the question is what Henry fastens on, and he builds a portrait of Samuel out of it. Passing through the gate Saul found him, and, little thinking this was Samuel himself, asked him the way to Samuel's house. See how mean a figure so great a man made: he took no state upon him, had no attendants, no ensigns of honour carried before him, nor any distinguishing habit — not even when he went up to worship — but appeared in all respects so much a common person that Saul, though he had been told he would meet him, never suspected it was he, and asked him the way to the seer's house as though he looked more like a porter than a prophet. Thus, Henry concludes, is great worth oftentimes hidden under a very despicable appearance.
19:
Samuel answers in four words, and Gill is careful about their tone: supposing from the enquiry after his house that the man's business was with him, he said this not as boasting of his character and office, nor in the pride and vanity of his mind, but merely for information's sake. Clarke reads it forward instead, as a preparation — the declaration would ready Saul for the communications afterwards made. Henry turns the exchange into a small parable: Samuel knew that it was not the house but the man that Saul wanted, and so answered, I am the seer, the person you enquire for. Samuel knew him before he knew Samuel; and so, though all who are called to the kingdom of glory are brought to know God, they were first known of him (Galatians 4:9).

Being told to walk in front is read two ways. Keil and Delitzsch say flatly that letting a person go ahead was a sign of great esteem, and Ellicott makes it a sign of distinguished honour from one of Samuel's rank to a young unknown wayfarer. Henry offers a homelier reason: Samuel bade him go before because it may be that some business obliged him to call somewhere by the way.

Both Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott notice that the Hebrew shifts number in the middle of the invitation. The command to go up is singular and addressed to Saul alone; the promise "ye shall eat" is plural, which Keil and Delitzsch explain on the ground that while Samuel spoke only to Saul he meant expressly to invite the servant to the meal as well; and then the words narrow again to Saul alone for the promise of disclosure. Ellicott traces the same movement sentence by sentence.

What Samuel undertakes to tell him is the one phrase here that needs deciding. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the obvious reading: "all that is in thine heart" does not mean all that lies heavy upon it, all that troubles thee, since Samuel relieves him of his anxiety about the asses at once by telling him they are found — it means simply the thoughts of his heart generally, which Samuel would make known to him in order to prove himself a prophet. Ellicott takes it the same way and enlarges it: on the morrow he would show this young Benjamite that he was indeed a seer, telling him all his secret thoughts and aspirations, while the asses were to be dismissed from his mind altogether, far graver matters than the everyday weal and woe of a farm on Mount Ephraim being reserved for the next day's conversation. Henry reads the whole detention as pastoral management. The greater part of the day had gone in sacrificing and the rest was to be spent in holy feasting, so Samuel keeps him till morning and no sooner; Saul had nothing in his mind but his father's asses, and Samuel meant to take him off that care and dispose him to the exercises of piety — let us pray together, and then we will talk together.
20:
The first thing Samuel does is settle the errand, and the reckoning of days draws a note. Gill reports Kimchi's view, which the Targum shares, that "three days ago" is counted not from the losing of the asses but from the time Saul had been looking for them — though Gill thinks it probable enough that he set out the same day they strayed. What matters, he adds, is the effect: Samuel told him of the asses and of the time so exactly, before Saul had said a word about either, which must at once convince him that this was a true prophet and prepare him to credit everything said afterwards. Henry makes the same inference and pushes it further: Samuel answered an enquiry Saul had not yet made and told him what he was thinking, from which he might reason that if a man of God can do this, much more does God himself understand our thoughts afar off. Clarke puts it in a line — he shows him that he knew what was in his heart.

The hint that follows is read two ways, and the difference is a matter of translation. Clarke and Wesley take "all the desire of Israel" to mean the thing Israel desires, namely a king, and Wesley extends the promise past Saul himself — the honour is designed for him and, after his death, for his family or posterity, if by his sin he does not cut off the entail. Ellicott denies that sense: the words do not signify what Israel desires but all that it possesses of what is precious or worth desiring, which is why the Latin renders it the best in Israel, as Luther did. On his reading the seer's obscure dark words were meant to draw Saul away from the asses and the small matters that had filled his life and lift him to higher thoughts; vague and indefinite as they were, coming from one so high in dignity, known to possess many a strange secret of futurity hidden from other men, and holding out a prospect of undreamed-of glory, they amazed the young man. Henry supplies the compliment buried in the question — is it not a king they are set upon, and is there a man in Israel who will suit them as thou wilt? — while noting that the country had as yet no eye upon Saul for the government, having left the choice wholly to God.

Saul's answer is taken as modesty by all three who comment on it, though they value it differently. Clarke calls the speech exceedingly modest and Saul now becomingly humble, and then asks the question the rest of the history answers: but who can bear elevation and prosperity? Henry thinks Saul supposed Samuel was bantering him, as a tall man but a very unlikely king, and notes that though the historian called his father a mighty man of power Saul himself speaks diminishingly of both tribe and family — Benjamin, the youngest of Jacob's sons, was called a little one even when grown (Genesis 44:20), the tribe was diminished by the war of Gibeah, and his own house was probably a younger one holding no place of honour even within it. Gideon had spoken in just that way (Judges 6:15), and a humble disposition, Henry says, is a good presage of preferment. Wesley and Clarke both explain the smallness as historical fact rather than modest fiction: the tribe had been cut down to six hundred men in the war with the other tribes, a blow it never recovered, so that it was scarcely reckoned an entire tribe but only the remnant of one — and being afterwards grafted into Judah it in some sort lost its name, the two being accounted but one tribe (Judges 20:46).
22:
Samuel never answers the protest, and Ellicott makes the silence deliberate: the seer gave no reply to the young man's wonder that one so insignificant should be chosen for so high a destiny, wishing in the first instance only to awaken new and grander thoughts in him, and so without a word he conducted his guests to the scene of the sacrifice.

Where he took them has an English name nobody likes. Ellicott calls "the parlour" an unfortunate rendering of a Hebrew word that signifies the cell or chamber attached to the building on the high place for just such purposes, those solemn sacrificial meals being the usual adjuncts of a solemn sacrifice. Keil and Delitzsch likewise render it the cell, the apartment prepared for the sacrificial meal. Gill calls it simply the dining room of the house belonging to the high place.

The seating is the point of the verse. Keil and Delitzsch note that the servant was given a place as well as his master, according to the simple customs of antiquity, as being also Samuel's guest, and that the thirty present were no doubt the most distinguished men of the city, the rest of the people encamping elsewhere. Ellicott has Samuel place the two, no doubt to their great surprise, in the principal seats, and adds a reflection on the servant's share: if tradition is right that this was Doeg the Edomite, he too had a foretaste here of the rank and power he would hold as one of Saul's great officers of state. Wesley sees the manoeuvre as public preparation — the chief place was given to raise the company's expectation and ready them to pay Saul the honour his approaching dignity required. Henry says the same and draws out what it cost the host: though Saul's advancement would be Samuel's own deposing, that good prophet was so far from envying him that he was the first and forwardest to do him honour, in compliance with the will of God — if this was the man God had chosen, then though he was none of Samuel's particular friends or confidants he was heartily welcome to his table, and to his bosom. Nor was a meal an unseasonable kindness, Henry adds, since by Saul's own account their provisions and money were spent. The magistrates were probably present and might in their own city have claimed precedence, yet the master of the feast set Saul above them, and the servant too, who if his master was to be king must be respected as a prime minister of state; from which Henry concludes that civil respects must be paid to those whom providence has given the precedency in civil things (Luke 14:9).

The order to the cook shows how far ahead the thing had been planned. Ellicott puts it plainly: everything that passed at the sacrificial feast and afterwards in Samuel's house had been arranged beforehand, every event foreseen and provided for down to the trivial details, all of it symbolic in a preparation for the great change in the constitution of Israel — the very piece of meat was no chance piece but one carefully set aside, being reckoned the choicest. Keil and Delitzsch say the same of the instruction, that Samuel ordered the cook to bring the piece he had directed him to set aside and place it before Saul. Clarke attends to the man rather than the dish: the word rendered cook is the masculine of the term used of the women cooks in Samuel's warning about a king, and comes from a root meaning to slay or butcher — so that probably the butcher is meant (1 Samuel 8:13).
24:
What was served with the shoulder nobody can settle. Keil and Delitzsch reject two readings before giving their own: not the broth poured over it, as Dathe and Maurer took it, and not the kidney as the choicest portion, as Thenius proposed — the kidneys of every slain sacrifice being burned upon the altar, with only the flesh coming to the meal (Leviticus 3:4) — but, with Luther, what was attached to the leg, which can only have been fat not destined for the altar. Gill lists the candidates: some think a sauce poured on it or a garnish about it, others the thigh, with the Targum and Jarchi and Kimchi, or rather, on an older Jewish authority, the breast, which adjoined the shoulder and went with it in the sacrifices. Clarke guesses the shoulder was covered with part of the caul so as to roast the better, and notes that the Targum gives the shoulder and its thigh — not the shoulder merely but the fore-leg bone down to the knee, perhaps the whole fore-quarter.

Which shoulder it was turns on who could dispose of it. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the text does not say, and that earlier commentators decided for the left because the right fell to the priests (Leviticus 7:32). Gill reports the same reasoning and argues past it: in those unsettled times much was dispensed with, and Samuel, though a Levite, might officiate as a priest, so that the right shoulder and breast belonged to him as such — which best accounts for his disposal of it, and for Saul, though no priest's son, being admitted to the choicest part as one designed to be king. Henry takes the other side and makes the left shoulder Samuel's own usual portion as the man at the upper end of the table, so that giving it to Saul was an implicit resignation of his place to him.

Why a shoulder is where the comment turns emblematic. Clarke denies it was set before Saul because it was the best part and says it was because it was an emblem of the government to which he was now called, pointing to the prophet's word that the government shall be upon his shoulder (Isaiah 9:6). Henry reads the pair of portions the same way: the shoulder denotes strength and the breast, which some think went with it, denotes affection — he that was king had the government upon his shoulder, for he must bear the weight of it, and the people in his bosom, for they must be dear to him.

Who speaks the closing words is a real question, and the answer changes the scene's tone. Wesley takes them for Samuel's, explaining that when he first said he had invited the people to join his sacrifice and share the feast, he then bade the cook reserve this part for Saul's use. Ellicott quotes Dean Payne Smith against that: Samuel's name is not in the Hebrew, and though the Greek and Latin insert it they do so by a manifest error, while the Syriac and Chaldee agree with the Hebrew in making the cook the speaker. On that reading the cook lifted the shoulder with what was upon it, set it before Saul, and said that what had been reserved was now set before him — eat, for it has been kept for thee unto the appointed time of which he spoke, saying, I have invited the people. The word rendered "since I said" means saying and nothing else, and nothing before it supplies a verb for that participle, so there is plainly an ellipse which the cook's speech resolves. The chat of the cook, Payne Smith adds, is entirely after the manner of ancient times, and would show Saul how completely his coming had been foreseen and provided for.
25:
The descent is a small geographical puzzle, and Gill solves it two ways. Though Ramah itself stood on an eminence, the high place seems to have been higher still, lying outside the city upon a hill, so that one came down from the one to the other; or else they came down from the high place and then climbed again to the town. The roof they went up to needs no explanation beyond the architecture: Clarke notes that all the houses of the East were flat-roofed, and that people walked, talked and frequently slept on them for the sake of the fresh and cooling air, while Keil and Delitzsch call such roofs the regular places of retirement for private conversation (Deuteronomy 22:8). Ellicott adds that the honoured guest was often lodged there for the night, and that Samuel detained Saul from continuing his journey and persuaded him to stay.

What they talked about that evening is flatly disputed. Wesley says it concerned the kingdom designed for him by God, and Henry fills the conversation out at length: Samuel now told him the whole story of the people's desire of a king, the grounds of it and God's granting of it, to all which Saul, living so privately, was perhaps a stranger, and satisfied him that he was the man God had pitched upon; and when Saul would object that Samuel was in possession and he would not take the government out of his hands, Samuel gave him every assurance of his willingness to resign. Keil and Delitzsch deny this outright. The conversation cannot have turned on the call to the royal dignity, since that was not made known to Saul as a word of Jehovah until the following day; it was meant to prepare him for the announcement. Ellicott agrees and, following Otto von Gerlach, supplies what the subject must have been instead — the sad religious and political decline of God's people, which Samuel had laboured not unsuccessfully to arrest, the opposition of the heathen nations, the causes of Israel's impotence against her enemies, the necessity of a religious change in the people, and the need of a leader thoroughly obedient to the LORD. That evening's talk, on this view, was the connecting link between the hint given on the height and the formal communication of the morning.

The Greek translators found the same difficulty and solved it by altering the text. Where the Hebrew has Samuel communing with Saul on the roof, Ellicott reports, they read that a couch was strewn for Saul on the roof and he lay down; the Chaldee and Syriac keep the Hebrew. He judges the variation apparently a correction, made because the translators could not understand a conversation in the evening when the announcement of the crown was made so formally next morning — and he lets the question stand that provoked it: why did Samuel not tell Saul of God's intention during that evening spent together?
26:
Whether either man slept is disputed. Gill reports Abarbinel's supposition that neither could — not Samuel, for thinking of what he had to do when morning came, which was to anoint Saul king over Israel; nor Saul, for the hint Samuel had dropped about the desire of all Israel being upon him, for the honour done him at the feast, and because of the conversation they had together afterwards. Ellicott says the opposite, and says it of Saul alone: evidently weary after the exciting scene and revelations of the day before, he slept soundly, probably heavily, on his couch spread on the roof of the prophet's house.

The rousing is a point of translation. Ellicott calls the English misleading, since it seems to suppose that they rose first and that Samuel called afterwards, about the spring of the day, whereas, as is frequent in Hebrew narration, the second clause relates the same event as the first with greater detail — it should run that they arose early, namely when the morning dawned, Samuel calling for Saul upon the roof. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way and locate the voices: Samuel called from below within the house up to the roof, where Saul was probably sleeping upon the balcony (2 Kings 4:10). Clarke makes the point most briskly — Saul had no doubt slept there all night, so there was no calling him to the house-top a second time; he was already there, and Samuel called him up.

The summons itself is rendered two ways, and the difference is not trivial. Ellicott keeps the English sense — get up, that I may send thee — while Keil and Delitzsch have Samuel say, Get up, I will conduct thee, which makes him not the one who dispatches Saul but the one who walks with him. Ellicott's own comment on the verse leans the same way: Samuel called from the roof-top in the early morning because he wished to conduct Saul himself out of the city, having a yet more important communication to make to his amazed and awe-struck visitor. What follows bears it out. As soon as Saul had risen, Keil and Delitzsch note, the two of them went out together into the street, Samuel and Saul and no one else, the servant left to be disposed of at the city's edge.
27:
The walk out of town is given a topography. Gill explains that the end of the city they were going down to was that end which led the way to the place where Saul was going, and that since the city stood on a hill, to go to its end was to go down a declivity, a descent. Clarke reads the opening clause as proof of how promptly Saul obeyed the summons from the roof: he arose immediately, and Samuel accompanied him out of the town rather than merely dismissing him at the door. Ellicott makes that escort the thing that must have struck Saul hardest. The honour and distinction already shown to him, a comparatively unknown Benjamite, by the famous prophet-judge was strange enough; the proposal to accompany him a little way on his journey homeward increased the wonderment.

The servant is sent ahead for the sake of privacy, and Wesley gives the reason behind the reason. Samuel wanted the two of them alone so that they might speak privately of the matter, or the kingdom — a thing Samuel had hitherto endeavoured to conceal, lest he should be thought to be imposing a king upon the people now, having before denied them one, and so that it might appear from the lot cast in the following chapter that the kingdom was given to Saul by God's destination and not by Samuel's contrivance. Ellicott puts the same arrangement in terms of the manner required rather than the suspicion avoided: the prophet directs that the servant be sent on alone so that he might in all solemn confidence impart to Saul the word of God. Keil and Delitzsch add nothing beyond the wording of the command itself — let the servant pass on before us, and do thou stand still a while.

What that word of God amounts to is glossed three ways, and the three do not pull against each other. Clarke takes it as the word, the counsel or design, of the LORD, and leaves the content to be discovered in the following chapter. Wesley defines it as a message delivered to me from God, which now I shall impart to thee. Ellicott is the fullest: all that the God of Israel had revealed to him, the seer, concerning Saul's appointment. The phrase, on each reading, covers not a general oracle but a particular disclosure that Samuel alone has been given and is now about to hand over.

Ellicott alone presses the question the narrative declines to answer. All that had happened the day before — the gracious welcome as a distinguished guest evidently looked for, the courteous hospitality in the judge's house, and more than all the long private instruction on the state of Israel given in the evening — was now to have its meaning revealed. It would have been interesting, he says, to have learned something of Saul's state of mind when this startling revelation of the choice of God was first made to him; but the writer here is silent. What Ellicott offers in place of the missing report is a principle drawn from the promise of the Spirit made to this chosen one in the next chapter: when new duties are imposed by God, He never forgets to bestow the gift of new powers.
